items.prompt: What's wrong with the assumption "working 20% more hours should produce roughly 20% more output"?
choices: Nothing — output genuinely does scale linearly with hours worked, at any level

Real output curves show diminishing returns (each added hour produces less than the last) and eventually negative returns (an added hour actively reduces total output) — the linear model only holds in a limited early range
The assumption is only wrong for creative work, never for technical work
Output only depends on total hours across a team's history, not weekly hours
items.explanation: The linear model tracks reality reasonably well at moderate hours, then diverges — first flattening (diminishing returns) and then, past a further point, actually declining (negative returns) as fatigue-driven mistakes and their rework cost outweigh the extra hours' direct output.

items.prompt: What's the practical difference between the "diminishing returns" and "negative returns" regions of the curve?
choices: There's no practical difference — both mean working more hours is always a bad idea

In diminishing returns, each extra hour still adds some output, just less than before — more hours is inefficient but not counterproductive; in negative returns, an extra hour actively reduces total output, making 'push harder' the wrong lever entirely
Diminishing returns only applies to physical labor, negative returns only to knowledge work
Negative returns means output becomes literally negative (below zero), which never happens in practice
items.explanation: This distinction is the practically important one from L2: diminishing returns still rewards more hours, just at a worsening rate, while negative returns means adding hours is actively working against the goal — crossing that boundary changes what the correct response should be.

items.prompt: Per L2's model, why does the effective-output curve bend downward rather than just flattening out?
choices: Because people work fewer total hours once they get tired
Because fatigue-driven mistakes create rework cost that's paid by FUTURE hours, not the hour that caused the mistake — so total net output can fall even as raw hours worked keeps climbing
Because companies enforce mandatory overtime caps
The curve never actually bends downward in real data — it only flattens
items.explanation: The key mechanism is that rework cost shows up on a different day than the fatigued hour that caused it — a model tracking only hours-worked-vs-direct-output misses this entirely, which is exactly why the effect is easy to underestimate in the moment.

items.prompt: Per L3's first failure mode, why is it risky to judge a crunch period's success using metrics like raw hours logged or raw lines of code written?
choices: These metrics are always fabricated during crunch periods

These raw activity metrics can keep climbing even in the negative-returns region, while net usable/shippable output is quietly falling behind them — the easy-to-measure numbers mask the number that actually matters
Raw hours and lines of code are the only metrics that matter, so this isn't actually risky
This only applies to teams without a code review process
items.explanation: L3 explicitly warns that visible activity metrics (hours, raw output) don't automatically track net usable output — in the negative-returns region they can diverge sharply, making a crunch look productive by the easy-to-see numbers while actually destroying value.

items.prompt: Why does L3 cite historical factory-labor data (Pencavel's analysis of WWI munitions plants) rather than relying only on modern knowledge-work examples?
choices: Because factory data is more precise and should be used as an exact benchmark for engineering teams today

Because it shows the diminishing-then-negative shape appears even in a domain with none of the 'maybe it's just knowledge-work' ambiguity — evidence the underlying mechanism (fatigue outweighing added time) isn't specific to modern tech work
Because no modern data on this topic exists
Because factory workers experience fatigue differently from knowledge workers, which the unit claims makes the comparison irrelevant
items.explanation: L3's last failure mode is explicit that the exact bend points from factory data shouldn't be over-applied as precise engineering benchmarks — the value of citing it is that the same qualitative shape (rising, then flat, then falling) shows up in an unrelated domain, supporting that the mechanism is general, not that the specific hour counts transfer directly.

items.prompt: Implement `weeklyOutput(hoursPerWeek, fatigueSensitivity)`, matching the interactive demo's formula: output equals `hoursPerWeek` minus a fatigue penalty. The penalty only applies to hours beyond a 50-hour baseline, and grows with the SQUARE of hours over that baseline, scaled by `fatigueSensitivity / 100`. The result should never go below 0.

tests.description: at or below 50 hours, there's no fatigue penalty
at exactly the 50-hour baseline, no penalty applies yet
past 50 hours, output falls below the raw hours worked
higher fatigue sensitivity produces a larger penalty for the same hours

items.explanation: This is the exact formula behind the interactive demo's chart: below the 50-hour baseline, output tracks hours one-to-one (the linear region); past it, the penalty grows quadratically, so the gap between raw hours and net output widens faster and faster — the mathematical shape of diminishing returns tipping into negative returns.
